title: Identify, describe, explain: what each verb really asks for
subtitle: Identify, describe and explain look alike. What does each one ask you to write, and how do you know you've actually explained?
subject: Chemistry and Biology
lessonIntent: answering one stimulus at three verb levels, and the s01 iron thiocyanate case at three levels; building a three-point explanation with linked causes; spotting a description posing as an explanation; two explain drills.

voiceover.text: In the last five years of HSC Chemistry and Biology papers, one key word came up in the written section more than any other: explain. Fifty-seven question parts, more than twice as many as the next word. Most were worth two to four marks. And every year, NESA's marking feedback mentions answers that say what happens, but not why. So let's sort out three verbs that look alike, but ask for different things.

Here's what NESA's glossary says, in short. Identify means recognise and name. Describe means give the features or characteristics. In plain words: what it's like, or what happened. Explain means show the cause and effect: how or why it happens. A fourth verb, outline, asks for the main features in general terms, a lighter describe. NESA also says to read each verb in its question, so let's use one.

Here's an HSC-style question. In fruit flies, eye colour depends on a gene on the X chromosome. A white-eyed female is crossed with a red-eyed male. Among the offspring, all 52 females have red eyes, and all 48 males have white eyes. Part a asks you to identify, part b to describe, and part c to explain. If you take Chemistry, you don't need the fly details. Watch what each verb makes the answer do.

Part a says identify, for one mark. So the answer is a name: the red allele is dominant. That's it. No reason is asked for, and a paragraph here only takes time from the parts that need it. When identify is worth two marks, read the question again: it may ask for two things.

Part b says describe, for two marks. Describe means saying what happened, with the features that matter. All 52 female offspring had red eyes, and all 48 males had white eyes. In other words, every daughter had her father's eye colour, and every son had his mother's. Use the numbers, and notice what's missing: there's no "because". Describe doesn't ask why.

Part c says explain, for three marks, and it asks why the males and females differ. So now you need causes. Three marks suggests about three linked points. And the content words tell you what to explain: males all white, females all red. A good explanation accounts for both. There's no constraint phrase this time, so any correct reasoning about the chromosomes counts.

Start from the cause. The eye-colour gene is on the X chromosome, and the Y has no copy of it. That's point one. A son gets his only X from his mother, and she has two white alleles. So every son has one white allele, with nothing to hide it, and he has white eyes. Point two. A daughter also gets her father's X, which carries the red allele. Red is dominant, so every daughter has red eyes. Point three. Each point says what causes what.

Now here's a weaker answer. "All the males had white eyes and all the females had red eyes, because the trait is sex-linked and males have only one X." The first half just repeats part b. Then it never says how it works: where each X comes from, for sons or for daughters. In our marking guide it earns one of three, for saying males have only one X. It described when the question said explain. Notice it even says because. A because isn't enough: it has to say how.

The same ladder works in Chemistry. Take the iron tube from the last video. Identify the colour after the crystals dissolve: deeper red. Describe what happens: the pale red solution turns a deeper red as the crystals dissolve. Explain it: with more iron three plus ions, they meet thiocyanate ions more often, so the forward rate rises above the reverse, and more of the red ion forms. Same tube, same chemistry. Only the verb changed, and it changed what earns the marks.

So here's a quick test. Read each sentence and ask: does it say what causes what? If it only says what happened, it's a description, however long it is. NESA's marking guidelines show the same step. In one recent three-mark explain question, about a disease-prevention campaign, outlining the campaign's features reached two marks, and only explaining its effect reached three. Explain questions run from two marks to seven. More marks means a longer chain, not a longer list.

Your turn. Do the one in your subject, or both. Chemistry first. A sealed bottle of soda water holds an equilibrium between carbon dioxide gas and dissolved carbon dioxide. When the cap is removed, bubbles form in the drink. Explain why. Three marks. Pause here to answer.

Removing the cap lets carbon dioxide gas escape, so there's less above the drink. Fewer gas molecules dissolve, so the dissolving rate falls, while leaving goes on at the same rate, at first. Leaving is now faster, so carbon dioxide comes out of solution as bubbles. A linked Le Chatelier answer works too. The habit to drop: "bubbles form because gas comes out of the drink." That just describes them.
Now Biology. When a DNA molecule is copied, the two new molecules are identical to each other. Assuming no copying errors, explain why. Two marks. Pause here to answer.

Two marks, two linked points. The strands separate, and each original strand is a template for a new one. Nucleotides join by complementary base pairing, A with T and C with G, so each new strand has the same sequence as the template's old partner, and both molecules get the original sequence. The habit to drop: "each has one old strand and one new strand." That says how they're built, not why the sequences match.

So, when you see the verb: identify, name what the question asks for, and use the marks to check how many. Describe, give the features, with numbers if there's data. Outline, the main features, briefly. Explain, show how each cause leads to its effect, step by step, and check every sentence says what causes what.
